newsitem.title: USA: Republicans raise more questions on Huang.
newsitem.headline: Republicans raise more questions on Huang.

text.p: Republicans raised more questions on Wednesday about John Huang, suspended as a fundraiser by the Democratic Party after reports he unlawfully solicited contributions, and his former employer, the Lippo Group of Indonesia.
Republican aides in the House of Representatives said Huang was given a security clearance at the Commerce Department without sufficient background checks.

Separately, Rep Bill Thomas, R-Calif., wrote to Democratic National Committee Chairman Christopher Dodd questioning a $1,000 contribution apparently made by Huang to Indiana Gov Evan Bayh's campaign on behalf of the Lippo Group of Indonesia on Dec. 19, 1995 when he was an employee on leave without pay from the Commerce Department.

In his letter to Dodd, a Democratic senator from Connecticut, Rep Thomas said that from Federal Election Commission records "it seems that in December of 1995 Mr Huang believed his employer was the Lippo Group, not the DNC or the Commerce Department."

Huang was suspended as a Democratic Party fundraiser after reports that he unlawfully solicited campaign contributions from a South Korean company. He worked for the Lippo Group before becoming a deputy assistant commerce secretary from mid-1994 through 1995.
He received the top secret security clearance in 1994 without any check on his work in Asia, staff aides of the House International Relations Committee said.

While he was with Lippo, Huang worked in Hong Kong for the Hong Kong Chinese Bank, then owned by Lippo and now jointly owned by Lippo and a company owned by the Chinese government, the Republican staff said.

Press reports and former Canadian intelligence official David Harris claimed that the company, China Resources (Holdings) Co., was an arm of China's Ministry of Foreign Trade that was involved in commmercial espionage.

On Huang's security clearance, a Republican staffer who asked that his name not be used, said: "There was no overseas component in his (Huang's) background check. It appears that what was done was the bare minimum." He said a foreign background check on Huang was requested but never performed.

In his government position, Huang got a weekly security briefing and had access to classified material, the staffers said. They said he was born in China, grew up in Taiwan and became a naturalised U.S. citizen in 1976.
The staffers released a Jan. 31, 1994, Commerce Department memo that gave Huang a waiver for an interim top secret clearance saying his expertise was critically needed at the Commerce Department.
Huang did not join the department until July 1994 and got his permanent security clearance that October.
